source.title: Information Guided Regularization for Fine-tuning Language Models
source.authors: Mandar Sharma; Nikhil Muralidhar; Sheng-Zhe Xu; Raquib Bin Yousuf; Naren Ramakrishnan

record.tranche_reason: Tests a different, information-guided dropout schedule against standard dropout and Gaussian dropout on downstream language tasks; it does not test the claim’s original image-classifier settings.
record.gate_note: The study compares guided dropout with standard and Gaussian dropout, but has no no-dropout condition. Figure 4 reports averages across five restarts and shows performance under smaller training cuts; exact figure values are not stated in the text. Table 2 is flattened: its cells do not clearly separate the reported Max and Mean values, so the displayed strings are preserved without assigning them to either statistic. Cited findings about sharp minima and prior regularizers are not this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study compares its guided dropout method with standard and Gaussian dropout during BERT fine-tuning. It has no no-dropout control and does not test whether adding dropout lowers error in the classifiers named by V6. Its loss-landscape visualizations do not measure the sharpness–generalization-gap relationship in V7. The batch-size discussion compares convergence with another study rather than testing V5 under controlled epoch budgets.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: Fisher-guided dropout improves BERT fine-tuning performance relative to standard dropout, including with reduced training data. The authors also claim broad task and architecture applicability and no added fine-tuning overhead, although downstream evaluations use BERT. Their claim of beating both baselines on nine of ten evaluations needs qualification: guided dropout loses to Gaussian dropout on MNLI mismatched for both statistics and on RTE for the mean.
record.recipe_differences: Information-guided layer-wise dropout during fine-tuning of pretrained BERTBASE; compared with standard and Gaussian dropout. Uses GLUE downstream tasks rather than the original claim’s natural-label image-classification and random-label memorization setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance is evaluated across GLUE tasks and progressively smaller training cuts for CoLA, MRPC, RTE, and STS-B; the text identifies batch size 8 versus 32 as the difference from the cited prior CoLA experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: Guided dropout improves the reported maximum and mean development scores over standard dropout on all ten Table 2 evaluation columns. Comparisons with Gaussian dropout are mixed on MNLI mismatched and RTE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fisher-guided layerwise dropout can improve BERTBASE fine-tuning performance relative to uniform dropout on GLUE.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 4 reports advantages for guided dropout over standard and Gaussian dropout across decreasing training-data cuts on four GLUE tasks; numerical figure values are unavailable in the supplied text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Guided dropout can outperform other dropout methods during BERT fine-tuning with limited task data.

fits_no_version.finding: Selective perturbation of high-Fisher parameters changes the visualized loss geometry of the same pretrained BERT model. No corresponding generalization gaps are measured.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fisher-ranked parameter subsets differ in their influence on BERT's visualized loss landscape.

fits_no_version.finding: All 30 BERTLARGE CoLA restarts at batch size 8 converged, whereas a cited study reported failures at batch size 32. There is no within-study batch-size comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: BERTLARGE fine-tuning convergence can differ across replication settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1 reports close agreement between Fisher estimates from the full WikiText-103 dataset and small subsamples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small corpus subsamples can approximate BERT's empirical Fisher information.

record.problems: Table 2 is flattened in the supplied text, leaving the Max and Mean values adjacent without a reliable separator. Figure 4 provides no exact values in its accompanying text. The study evaluates BERTBASE on GLUE, does not include a no-dropout condition, and reports results averaged across five restarts with inter-quartile ranges only for Figure 4.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure 4’s exact values are not stated in the text and were not reconstructed from the figure.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Controlled batch-size comparisons of held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.

Whether adding dropout lowers held-out error; small-dataset and excessive-dropout limits; removing dropout and weight decay with augmentation. Only dropout-method comparisons in pretrained transformers are reported.
Whether magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance ranks measured generalization gaps across comparably fitted networks, including comparisons with norm and margin measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Table 2's caption specifies maximum followed by mean, making the concatenated values separable. A small advantage between two dropout methods does not establish a partial V6 effect, and inferior comparator performance does not challenge V6. No verdict labels apply to any supplied version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets.

A no-dropout comparison; fully connected or convolutional classifiers; the stated very-small-training-set and excessive-dropout limits; removing dropout and weight decay together with data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance measured against training-test gaps and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.
